title: Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill 2014
short_title: Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill 2014

divisions.question: Rob Mitchell In accordance with standing order 133(b), I shall now proceed to put the question on the motion moved by the Minister for Agriculture on which a division was called for and deferred in accordance with standing orders. No further debate is allowed. Question put.

speeches.speaker: Joel Fitzgibbon
speeches.brief: Argued against the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, saying the government's promised $100 million boost for research corporations is undermined by $80 million cut from cooperative research centres, $146 million cut from CSIRO and $11 million cut from the Rural Industries Research and Development Corporation, breaching pre-election commitments.

speeches.speaker: Gary Gray
speeches.brief: Argued against the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill 2014 as an unnecessary attempt to save a paltry $7 million over four years from research and development corporations, noting Western Australia's grain crop, mostly exported through the Kwinana terminal, typically runs to 12 million to 18 million tonnes a year and remains dependent on strong RDC-backed science.

speeches.speaker: Cathy McGowan
speeches.brief: Argued that the government should not change the rural research and development corporation funding model without proper industry consultation, backing the National Farmers Federation's call for a five-year sunset clause, and cited a 2012 study finding Australia needed 4,000 professionally qualified agricultural researchers but produced only 800.

speeches.speaker: Eric Hutchinson
speeches.brief: Supported the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, welcoming an extra $100 million over four years for rural research and development corporations to be leveraged with universities and industry, and highlighted the Tasmanian Institute of Agriculture's irrigation research program as a model, noting two-thirds of Australian agricultural product is exported.

speeches.speaker: Justine Elliot
speeches.brief: Opposed the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill, arguing it was another unfair budget measure shifting membership costs onto research and development corporations, and cited an $80 million reduction in cooperative research centre funding and more than $100 million in CSIRO cuts costing around 500 jobs, noting each research dollar typically returns $10.

speeches.speaker: Clare O'Neil
speeches.brief: Opposed the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill, describing it as a cut to agricultural research and development spending and part of a broader pattern of cuts to research funding in Australia, and said her focus would be on the bill's impact on rural people, employment and productivity.

speeches.speaker: Tony Pasin
speeches.brief: Supported the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, contrasting his own vast regional electorate with the opposition member's 75 square kilometre seat, criticising Labor's fiscal record by noting close to $800 million a month in interest payments goes to overseas entities, and welcomed the Minister for Agriculture's appointment of six new members to the Rural Industries Research and Development Corporation.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: Opposed the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill, citing a $146.8 million cut to CSIRO funding expected to cost about 500 jobs, an $11 million reduction to the Rural Industries Research and Development Corporation, and an $80 million cut to the Cooperative Research Centres Program, and linked these to the closure of Melbourne University's Dookie agricultural campus.

speeches.speaker: Ken O'Dowd
speeches.brief: Supported the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill, welcoming a $100 million government investment in agricultural research, and illustrated the gap between farm gate and retail prices by noting a kilogram of rump steak might sell for $20 to $25 while the beef producer receives as little as $1.25 to $2.25.

speeches.speaker: Keith Pitt
speeches.brief: Argued in support of the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill, which will save about $7 million over four years by having 15 rural research and development corporations pay international membership fees directly, and raised concerns about biosecurity risks from lifting a ban on fresh ginger imports from Fiji.

speeches.speaker: Michael McCormack
speeches.brief: Argued in support of the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill, citing an ABARES estimate that every dollar the government invests in agricultural research returns $12 to farmers within 10 years, and announced $10.8 million for grains research in New South Wales creating 18 new research offices, including in Wagga Wagga and Yanco.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: Argued in support of the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill, citing studies showing every dollar invested in rural research returns $2.36 over five years and $5.56 over 10 years, and said the government spends $250 million a year on rural research including a new $100 million R&D-for-profit program.

speeches.speaker: Nola Marino
speeches.brief: Argued in support of the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill, saying an extra $100 million on top of the existing $250 million committed to rural R&D would help farmers stay competitive, and said productivity growth in the farm sector has outpaced the rest of the economy.

speeches.speaker: John Cobb
speeches.brief: Argued in support of the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill, defending the government's extra $100 million commitment to rural R&D and criticising the previous government's Productivity Commission inquiry, which had proposed cutting matching R&D funding for agriculture by about 50 per cent.

speeches.speaker: Luke Hartsuyker
speeches.brief: Argued in support of the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill, saying it would save about $7 million over four years by having research corporations pay their own international membership fees, and highlighted growth in his electorate's blueberry industry, including the Oz Berries cooperative's 20 per cent annual production growth.

speeches.speaker: Luke Hartsuyker
speeches.brief: Argued that employment service providers had been spending up to 50 per cent of their time on paperwork, and said the new employment services contract starting 1 July 2015 would significantly cut red tape, tying this commitment to the Rural Research and Development Legislation Amendment Bill's own deregulation aims.
